Not off limits, but it needs approval. Friday deploys require approval from the on-call engineering manager [1][2]. The normal deploy window is Monday through Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific [1][2].

A few other rules apply:

- **Billing freeze:** Ledger is under a month-end freeze from Friday, October 30, until invoices are sent (expected November 2). No normal changes to Ledger during that window [4]. Since it's Saturday now, that freeze is still in effect if your deploy touches Ledger.
- **Canary bake:** Every deploy goes to a canary cell first. It now stays there 45 minutes before automatic promotion, up from 20 [2]. A typical non-data-plane change reaches all cells about 50 minutes after merge [2].
- **Data-plane changes:** Changes under `ingest/` or `runner/` roll out in waves, about two and a half hours in total [2].
- **Rollbacks:** Always allowed without approval, including during freezes [1][2][3].
- **Normal changes:** Schema migrations, infrastructure config, retention settings, and auth or billing logic need sign-off from the owning team's change approver [3]. Those approvals are valid for 7 days [3].

A critical lab result must reach the ordering clinician within **60 minutes** [1]. If you can't reach the ordering clinician within **30 minutes**, the result goes to the **medical director on call** [1].

To reach the on-call medical director, call the Halcyon answering service at **555-0144** and choose **option 2**. Don't text physicians' personal mobile numbers, because pages through the answering service are logged and timed, which the chart documentation needs [2].

Record every critical result notification in the chart with the time and the person notified [1].

Separately, the escalation protocol says a critical lab value called in by the reference lab requires notifying the supervising physician within 30 minutes [1]. The 60-minute and 30-minute figures above are from the critical-results section, so check with your clinic if you're unsure which applies to a specific call.

Emergency access to a customer workspace lasts **2 hours**, and a second engineer must approve it [1].

**Approval steps**
1. Run `nwctl access request --workspace <id> --reason <case-or-incident-id>`. Every request must reference an open support case or declared incident [1].
2. A second engineer from the support or on-call rotation approves the request in Teleport. You can't approve your own request, and the approver can't be on the same case [1].
3. Access is read-only by default. Write access, such as editing a pipeline, needs the customer's written consent recorded in the case first [1].

If you need more time, submit a new request with an update on the case. The 2-hour limit is deliberately shorter than the standard 8-hour Teleport production session [1][2]. All sessions are recorded [2].

rows.answer:
No. Removing the name is not enough, and you shouldn't paste the history into a public chatbot or any general-purpose AI assistant.

- **Treat it as PHI.** Halcyon's approved-tools list says "de-identified" is not a loophole, because removing a name does not make a case non-identifiable [1].
- **Public and general-purpose AI tools are not approved.** The list excludes public chatbots and general-purpose AI assistants on any device, including personal phones [1]. The HIPAA policy says PHI must never go into AI tools that are not on the approved list [1][2].
- **Halcyon Assist won't work either.** It is for policy questions only, and you shouldn't paste patient details into it even without names [1].

What you can use:
- **Quillon Ambient** is the approved AI scribe. It drafts visit notes and is limited to the Riverside and Elm Park pilot clinics, with patient verbal consent and clinician review of every note [1][3].
- **Meridian draft replies** drafts patient portal responses inside the EHR. A clinician must edit or approve each one before it is sent [1].
- For a summary of a patient's history, the approved route is the Meridian EHR, which holds the full clinical record [4].

If you think a different AI tool would help your work, the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) handle approval. It requires a security risk assessment, a signed BAA, an inventory entry, and, for clinical use, a CMIO safety review. Turnaround is typically 6–10 weeks [1].

**17 lab results** from Bayline Reference Laboratories were filed into the wrong patient's chart at the Riverside and Northgate clinics between July 21 and 23, 2026 [1]. Two patients had abnormal results go to another chart, and their follow-up was delayed by four and six days. Neither suffered lasting harm [1].

The root cause analysis (RCA-26-07) identified a chain of failures [1]:

- **Unannounced feed change:** On July 20, Bayline changed its results feed and moved the medical record number (MRN) into a different HL7 segment, without notice [1].
- **Fallback matching:** Switchyard could no longer find the MRN and fell back to a matching rule based on last name and year of birth only. That rule had existed since 2021 and had never been used at volume [1].
- **No monitoring:** Nobody was alerted that 100% of Bayline results were using the fallback rule [1].
- **No change-notice obligation:** The Bayline agreement did not require advance notice of feed format changes [1].

A medical assistant at Riverside caught the problem on July 23 when a potassium result didn't match the patient's history. The feed was stopped, and the MRN mapping was corrected and the feed restored on July 24 [1]. All 17 results were moved to the correct charts by July 24 [1].

A related action item, Project Heron, adds a positive patient identification check before lab results are released to the patient portal. It is listed as built and awaiting release, targeted for Q4 2026 [6].

Halcyon doesn't use a five-business-day postmortem window. Its equivalent is a **root cause analysis (RCA) completed within 45 calendar days** of the event becoming known. Every Level 1 and Level 2 event gets one [1].

The related timelines are:

- **Charter:** QPS charters the RCA team within 72 hours [1].
- **Completion:** the RCA is due within 45 calendar days of the event becoming known [1].
- **Review:** completed RCAs and their action plans go to the Patient Safety Committee, chaired by the Chief Medical Officer, Dr. Kenji Watanabe. The committee meets monthly and tracks every action item to closure [1].

For a recent example, RCA-26-07 covered lab results filed to the wrong chart, with events on July 21–23, 2026 and the RCA completed August 28, 2026 [4]. That is within the 45-day window from the July 23 discovery.

The knowledge base doesn't use the term "incident commander." The closest equivalent is the **charge nurse**, who coordinates the immediate response to a patient safety event. If there is no charge nurse on shift, the **clinic manager** takes that role.

- **Clinic managers:** In clinics without a charge nurse on shift, staff tell the clinic manager, who then coordinates the response [1][2]. Clinic managers for each site are listed in the clinic directory [4].
- **Sentinel events:** The charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour [1]. The on-call medical director is the senior physician on duty for the network, reached through the answering service at 555-0144, option 2 [3].

Halcyon needs a **signed business associate agreement (BAA)** before any patient data goes to a vendor. The security review is a separate requirement that runs alongside it. Halcyon's documents call the contract a BAA, not a DPA.

**What's required**

- **Signed BAA first.** Under the HIPAA privacy policy, a vendor that will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI on Halcyon's behalf is a business associate. No PHI may be disclosed until the BAA is executed, and that includes test files or "just a few names" for a pilot [1].
- **Security risk assessment.** Any tool that will handle PHI needs one [2]. Halcyon's Tallgrass record shows the assessment was done and passed with conditions, but the BAA was still unsigned, so no data could flow yet [1].
- **Entry in the clinical and business systems inventory.** This inventory lists the systems approved to hold PHI. It is maintained by the HIPAA Security Officer, Ahmed Siddiqui [6][2].
- **Clinical safety review by the CMIO, for clinical use.** This applies to AI tools [2]. Quillon Ambient's expansion beyond its pilot clinics, for example, needs a CSCAB decision and a clinical safety review [4].

**Who to contact:** For AI tools, email the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui). Typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [2].

**Example:** Tallgrass Survey Co. has a passed security assessment but no executed BAA. Its order form is on hold, and the team is still negotiating retention terms [1].

rows.answer:
Northwind has no EHR, so it has no direct equivalent of Meridian break-the-glass. Its closest match is emergency access to customer workspaces, which is a similar "get into restricted data outside normal permissions" control, but it is built differently [7].

**Halcyon (Meridian EHR)**
- Users are normally limited to charts they have a treatment, payment, or operations relationship with. Break-the-glass lets them open a chart outside that limit when care requires it [1].
- The user picks a reason (Emergency care, Coverage, or Other), writes a justification, and gets access until the end of the shift, up to 12 hours [1].
- No one approves it in the moment; care comes first [1].
- Every event is logged and reviewed by the Privacy Officer's team within 2 business days. Managers may be asked to confirm unclear reasons [1].
- Misuse is a privacy incident and can lead to termination [1]. Looking up family, coworkers, public figures, or yourself is never allowed [1][2].

**Northwind (customer workspaces)**
- Access requires an open support case or declared incident, and every request must cite that ID. "Curiosity" or "it would be faster" are not valid reasons [7].
- A second engineer from support or on-call must approve it in Teleport. The approver cannot be on the same case [7].
- Access is read-only by default. Write access needs the customer's written consent in the case first [7].
- It expires after 2 hours, shorter than the standard 8-hour production session [7][8].
- Sessions are recorded and kept for a year. Enterprise admins are emailed within 24 hours, and Security reviews a sample of sessions weekly, plus every session that used write access [7].
- Restricted data cannot be exported or pasted into tickets or Slack [7].

**Key differences**
- **Approval:** Halcyon has none before access and relies on after-the-fact review. Northwind requires a second engineer to approve before access starts.
- **Justification:** Halcyon uses a self-selected reason and free text. Northwind ties access to a case or incident ID.
- **Duration:** Halcyon allows up to 12 hours. Northwind allows 2 hours and requires a new request to extend.
- **Scope:** Halcyon's access is read-write for the chart. Northwind's is read-only unless the customer consents to writes.
- **Notification:** Northwind notifies the customer's admins. Halcyon's sources do not mention notifying patients.

The two are not directly comparable, since one covers clinical records and the other covers customer data in a software platform. The main lesson from Northwind's design is the up-front second approval and the shorter window, which Halcyon's policy does not include.

**Northwind: sometimes, depending on the data. Halcyon: never, for patient data.**

**Northwind Labs**
- Restricted data never goes in Slack. That covers customer event payloads, credentials and encryption keys [1]. Support must also use field names and counts instead of pasting payloads into Slack [4].
- Confidential data (financials, contracts, employee data) is allowed on a need-to-know basis [1]. The policy doesn't explicitly say Slack is the channel for it, so check with your team if you're unsure.
- Internal and Public data can be shared freely [1].

**Halcyon Health**
- PHI never goes in Slack, including DMs [2][3]. The same rule covers email subject lines, personal notes apps, and AI tools that aren't on the approved list [3].
- For patient communication, use the EHR's secure messaging. For email to outside providers, use encrypted email with `[secure]` in the subject line [3].

If you accidentally see data you shouldn't, at Northwind report it in `#security-help` [4]. The Northwind policy says good-faith reports are never penalized [1].

- **PR process:** add the `change:normal` label, fill in the risk and rollback sections, and request the approver as a CODEOWNERS reviewer, plus `@northwind/security` for Restricted services [1]. Approvals expire after 7 days [1].
- **Freezes:** the holiday freeze runs December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027, and only standard and emergency changes are allowed then [1].

The service is **Ledger**, which is owned by the **Identity & Billing (IDB)** team [5]. If Harriet Vance is out, her delegate is **Arjun Mehta** [4].

The duplicate invoices came from Ledger's month-end invoicing job. A retry re-ran a batch after a payment-provider webhook timed out, and invoice creation wasn't idempotent. That caused 312 duplicate invoices across 287 workspaces under incident INC-2340 [2]. An idempotency key per workspace and billing period shipped on October 8 [1][3].

Two timing notes:
- A month-end billing freeze on Ledger runs from Friday, October 30, until invoices are sent, expected November 2. No normal Ledger changes are allowed in that window [3].
- Harriet and Arjun are both out November 24–27. Changes planned around that week should either avoid it or use the exceptions route in the production change approval policy [3]. I didn't look up that policy, so I can't say what the exceptions route requires.

By default, Northwind keeps archived event payloads for **365 days** in Driftwood, the cold store. This comes from the v2 retention standard, effective September 15, 2026 [2]. It replaced v1, which set the default at 400 days [1][2].

- **Enterprise contracts:** Customers can contract for a shorter archive period [1]. Under v2, they can also contract for longer retention, up to 730 days, with security team approval [2].
- **Enforcement:** Object-storage lifecycle rules delete archived objects once they pass the retention period for their workspace. Per-workspace overrides are stored as bucket tags [2].
- **Hot buffer:** Event payloads in Kafka are kept for 7 days, separate from the archive [2].

Enterprise workspaces are specified for reference tables of up to **500 million rows per workspace** [1]. The source is a product spec for streaming joins, so treat this as the design target rather than a confirmed production limit.

Some context on where Tributary stands:

- The streaming-joins spec lists 50 million rows per workspace for Growth and 500 million for Enterprise [1].
- Tributary is in private beta with design partners, and its GA target is January 2027 [4].
- Snapshot restore work was scoped around a 50M-row table, with a target restore time under 90 seconds [2]. I found no source that confirms performance at the 500M-row level.

For a contractual or go-live figure, check with the Tributary product team.

rows.answer:
When a customer goes over the limit, the API returns **HTTP 429**, and the response includes a **`Retry-After`** header that gives the number of seconds to wait [1].

**What they get back**
- Status code 429 on the rejected request [1].
- A `Retry-After` header with the wait time in seconds [1].
- Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota [1].

**How they know when to retry**
- The `Retry-After` header tells them how long to wait [1].
- Northwind's SDKs honor that header automatically and back off exponentially [1].
- The source doesn't say whether raw HTTP clients that don't use the SDKs get any extra guidance, so customers calling the API directly should read `Retry-After` and wait that long before retrying.

**Useful context**
- Limits are per workspace, not per API key. Ten keys in one workspace share one budget [1].
- Short bursts up to 2x the limit are allowed for 10 seconds [1].
- Limits differ by endpoint and plan. For example, event ingest (`POST /v2/events`) is 100 req/s on Starter, 2,000 req/s on Growth, and 10,000 req/s on Enterprise by default [1].
- Endpoints that aren't included in a customer's plan return HTTP 403, not 429 [1].

The source is the internal rate-limit page, which says the public docs copy it on each release [1].

rows.answer:
You need sign-off from **PLAT's change approver**. Hydrant is owned by PLAT, and its per-cell floors and ceilings live in the PLAT infrastructure repo. Changing a ceiling is a normal change under the infrastructure-configuration rules, so it needs that approver's sign-off [1][6]. You don't need security sign-off, because Hydrant stores no customer data and isn't a Restricted service [1].

To request it, add the `change:normal` label to the PR, fill in the risk and rollback sections, and request review from the approver as a CODEOWNERS reviewer. Approvals are valid for 7 days [6]. I didn't find the approver's name in the knowledge base, so check the engineering team directory [6].

The us-east cell currently has a Hydrant floor of 16 and a ceiling of 64 gateway replicas [2].

Two things to consider before you file:
- If a cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes, Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call, because hitting the ceiling usually means a gateway problem rather than real traffic [1]. Check for a gateway fault before assuming you need more capacity.
- If you only need to pin the replica count temporarily, for example while debugging, use `nwctl hydrant hold --cell <cell> --replicas <n> --ttl 2h`. Holds need no approval, but they last at most 4 hours [1].

The $1,200-a-month plan is the Growth plan [2]. On Growth, the bulk endpoint `POST /v2/events/batch` allows **50 requests per second** and up to **10,000 events or 10 MB per request** [1].

- **Rate:** 50 req/s per workspace, not per API key. Short bursts up to 2x (100 req/s) are allowed for 10 seconds [1].
- **Size:** 10,000 events or 10 MB per request, whichever the request hits first [1].
- **Over the limit:** the API returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header. Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota [1].

For a one-year backfill, Growth customers can ask for a temporary raise. The DP on-call primary can grant a one-off backfill raise of up to 72 hours on any plan that has the endpoint [1]. Growth limits are otherwise fixed by contract, and customers who need more are pointed to Enterprise [1].

A deploy sits in the canary cell for **45 minutes** before it can be promoted automatically [1]. This is a change from the 20 minutes in the Engineering Handbook. The October 2026 pipeline note says it overrides the handbook where they differ, and the handbook will be updated to match [1][2].

Promotion also requires two additional checks during the bake, on top of the existing error-rate and p95 latency checks (within 10% of baseline) [1]:
- Zero sustained TLS handshake errors between gateways and brokers in canary.
- Runner consumer lag not growing by more than 2 minutes during the bake.

Someone can hold a deploy in canary with `/deploy hold <deploy-id>` in Slack. It stays there until someone runs `/deploy release` or rolls it back [1]. You can check progress and remaining time with `nwctl deploy status` [1].

rows.answer:
No, don't run `nwctl scale ingest` by hand in us-west. Hydrant, the new gateway autoscaler, has managed us-west replicas since October 15 [2]. The runbook's manual scaling step is outdated, and Hydrant will revert a manual change within 2 minutes [2].

What to do instead:

- **Let Hydrant scale.** It adds replicas when average gateway CPU stays above 65% for 3 minutes, so 80% CPU should already trigger it [2]. It does not scale in the first 10 minutes after a gateway deploy [2].
- **Pin a count only if you need to**, for example while debugging a bad gateway build: `nwctl hydrant hold --cell <cell> --replicas <n> --ttl 2h`. Holds last at most 4 hours and need no approval. Release early with `nwctl hydrant release --cell <cell>` [2].
- **Watch for the ceiling.** If the cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes, Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call, because that usually means a gateway problem rather than real traffic [2]. I didn't find the us-west ceiling value in the knowledge base. It's listed in the production cell inventory.
- **Check the rest of the runbook.** Confirm which cell is affected and look at gateway TLS handshake errors first [1][2]. INC-2291 was a TLS handshake failure that looked like a capacity problem in a different cell, and it took 89 minutes to diagnose because the failure was on the client side [5].

The request rate limit for the legacy `POST /v1/track` endpoint on a Growth plan is **500 requests per second** [1]. Each request can carry up to 100 events [1].

The limit applies per workspace, not per API key, so all keys in one workspace share the same budget. Short bursts of up to 2x the limit are allowed for 10 seconds, and requests over the limit get HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header [1].

This endpoint is being retired: it stops accepting events on April 30, 2027, and SDKs released after March 2025 already use `/v2/events` [2].

Enterprise workspaces can force a reference-table snapshot rebuild **once every 2 minutes** through `POST /v2/reference-tables/{id}/refresh` [1]. The default Growth limit is 1 per 10 minutes, and Starter has no access to the endpoint at all, returning HTTP 403 [1].

The limit is per workspace, not per API key, so all keys in one workspace share the same budget [1]. Going over the limit returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header [1].

The source also notes that a forced refresh discards the runner's snapshot and rebuilds it with a full table scan, which is expensive for large tables. It adds that most customers never need it because snapshots are kept current with change data capture [1].

The policy gives you a 14-day grace period after the January 31 deadline, so the lockout date depends on which deadline you mean.

- **If you mean the January 31, 2027 deadline:** access is suspended automatically if training is more than 14 days overdue, so you would be locked out after about February 14, 2027 [1].

The policy says training is due "annually by January 31" [1]. I couldn't find a source that says whether the suspension is applied automatically in practice or how you would get access back, so check with your manager or compliance to confirm your training status and your due date.

rows.answer:
No, don't throw the vaccines out yet. Halcyon's policy says that when a vaccine fridge reads outside 2–8 °C, you must keep the stock and get a pharmacist's decision first [1].

Here's what the policy requires:

1. **Don't discard anything.** Label the affected stock "Do not use," keep it refrigerated in a working unit, and record the reading, the time, and how long it has been out of range [1].
2. **Call the clinical pharmacist within 1 hour.** The pharmacist checks with the manufacturers whether the stock can still be used [1].
3. **File a SafeReport.** It's a Level 4 near miss if no vaccine was given. It's a higher level if a patient received affected vaccine [1][2].
4. **Don't give any vaccine from the affected stock** until the clinical pharmacist releases it in writing [1].

Frozen vaccines are never refrozen or reused after thawing [1].

If a patient is unwell or has received vaccine from this fridge, follow the clinical escalation protocol and tell the charge nurse or clinic manager right away [2][3].

Halcyon's standard is **10 business days** to provide a copy of the record when it isn't available instantly in the portal. HIPAA allows up to 30 calendar days, so 10 business days is the internal target [1].

- **Portal download:** free and immediate. Point the patient there first, since visit notes, results and immunizations are usually available [1].
- **Electronic copy (secure email or encrypted USB) or paper:** $6.50 flat fee, 10 business days [1].
- **Sensitive records,** such as substance use treatment records, are released only after the Privacy Officer reviews the request [1].
- **Unpaid balances** can't delay the request [1].

Requests are logged in the HIM request queue in Meridian EHR [1]. The HIM supervisor is Joanna Kowalczyk [1].

**Short answer:** Keep trying the ordering clinician for up to 30 minutes. If you still can't reach them, the result goes to the on-call medical director. The whole notification must reach the ordering clinician within 60 minutes [1].

**Steps:**

1. **Try the ordering clinician for 30 minutes.** The protocol requires the result to reach the ordering clinician within 60 minutes, and sends it to the medical director if that clinician cannot be reached in 30 minutes [1]. The sources don't describe how to attempt contact during those 30 minutes.
2. **Escalate to the on-call medical director.** The on-call medical director receives critical lab results when the ordering clinician can't be reached [2]. Call the Halcyon answering service at 555-0144 and choose option 2. The service pages the on-call medical director and pages the backup if there is no callback within 10 minutes. Don't text physicians' personal mobile numbers [2].
3. **Document everything.** Record the time and the person notified in the chart for each critical result notification [1].

Probably not today. Elmhurst is not a hub clinic, so it does not normally stock the shingles vaccine.

- The recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV) is Tier 2, which means it is stocked at hub clinics only. Other clinics request a transfer from the nearest hub, and transfers arrive within 2 business days [1].
- Elmhurst is not a hub [2]. Its Saturday hours are 09:00–12:00 [2].
- RZV can be given by an RN or clinician, not an MA [1]. Saturday sessions require one physician or NP on site but no RN [5], so confirm an RN or clinician is available before booking.
- Eligibility is ages 50 and over. The series is two doses, given 2–6 months apart, at $205 per dose for self-pay patients [1]. The prompt-pay discount does not apply to vaccine prices, though sliding-fee patients get the program discount [1].

Practical next steps: confirm the patient's age, ask the nearest hub (Northgate or Harbor Point, per the directory's hub list [2]) whether it can transfer stock, and book the first dose for when the transfer arrives. If the patient wants today's visit, Elmhurst can still do the consult and schedule the vaccine. I did not find a document that shows which hub is nearest to Elmhurst, so check that with Clinical Operations.

Riverbend should be scheduling **1.5 medical assistants per clinician** under the current standard. Riverbend's band is Medium, and the rule is rounded up to the next whole person.

- **Current standard:** The clinic staffing standard effective September 1, 2026 replaced the 2025 version [1].
- **Riverbend's band:** Riverbend averaged 46 visits a day in Q3 2026 [3]. The Medium band covers 40 to 80 visits a day [1]. The 2026 standard sets Medium at 1.5 MAs per clinician, with at least 2 physicians or NPs on site [1].
- **Practical result:** With one physician or NP, that is 2 MAs (1.5 rounded up). With two, it is 3 MAs. Medium clinics also need 1 RN on site and 3 front desk staff [1].

Under the 2025 standard, Riverbend's Medium band was 1.25 MAs per clinician [2], so the requirement went up. The band is recalculated quarterly from the clinic directory's visit column, so it could change if volume shifts [1][3].

If Bayline's results feed stops arriving, Bayline has **30 minutes** to give a first response. That is a contractual first response from a qualified engineer, not a resolution time. Results not arriving is listed as a P1 example, and Bayline's support runs 24/7 through its interface desk [2].

The Halcyon person paged is the **system steward for Integration Services (INT), Owen Mbeki** [8]. The process runs like this:

- Open a ticket with the Halcyon IT Service Desk (extension 4357, or the intranet tile). Clinic staff should not call Bayline directly unless the Service Desk asks them to [2].
- For any P1, the Service Desk contacts Bayline and also pages the owning team's steward, which here is Owen Mbeki [2][8].
- If Bayline misses the 30-minute P1 response, the Service Desk escalates to Bayline's account manager and tells the steward. Two missed P1 responses in one quarter are reported to the HIPAA Security Officer [2].

Because the feed is a patient-safety risk, the charge nurse on shift should also be told and should file a SafeReport, as in the 2026 Bayline incident where the feed was stopped [1][4].

A large clinic needs **2.0 medical assistants per clinician** on the schedule under the current standard. Round up to the next whole person [1].

- **Large clinic:** more than 80 average visits per day, with 3 physicians or NPs on site minimum, 2 RNs on site (one designated charge nurse), and 4 front desk staff minimum [1].
- **Counting:** "MAs per clinician" means the number of MAs scheduled for each physician or NP seeing patients [1].
- **Which clinic is large:** the band is set from the "Avg visits per day" column in the clinic directory, recalculated every quarter [1][3].

This replaces the 2025 standard, which set large clinics at over 90 visits a day and 1.5 MAs per clinician [2]. The 2026 revision was made because medium and large clinics were missing door-to-room targets on most afternoons [1].

No. Under the current standard, every clinic, including small clinics, must have at least one RN on site during open hours, and Saturday sessions also need an RN [1]. The 2025 standard did not require an RN in small clinics [2], but it was replaced on September 1, 2026 [1].

If a session can't be covered with an RN, the clinic manager calls the float pool first. A session run without an RN must be reported in SafeReport as a near miss so QPS can track it [1].

rows.answer:
Northwind doesn't have a PHI-specific inventory in the knowledge base, but its **service catalog** is the closest equivalent. It lists each production service, what data it stores, a data class, and the owning team. The Platform team maintains it [9].

**How it works at Northwind**

- The catalog says which team owns each service and what data it keeps. Restricted and Confidential classes follow the data classification table in the information security policy [9][12].
- Owners appear as team codes. The engineering team directory maps each code to its engineering manager and named change approver [15].
- To change an owner, you open a PR against the catalog and tag both the old and new engineering managers [9].
- Adding a new datastore requires an ADR before the service appears in the catalog [9].

rows.answer:
At Halcyon, patient safety events go into **SafeReport**. Anyone involved in or who witnessed the event files the report, and the policy says reporting is never optional and never punished [1]. The policy doesn't give a filing deadline for the SafeReport entry itself. The 24-hour and 1-hour timings below come from the policy's immediate-response steps.

**Who does what:**
- **Anyone involved or who witnessed the event** files the SafeReport entry [1].
- **The charge nurse on shift** is told first. In clinics without one, the clinic manager is told. The charge nurse coordinates the immediate response [1].
- **The charge nurse** notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour for a sentinel event [1]. The on-call director is reached through the answering service at 555-0144, option 2 [3].
- **The attending clinician** discloses the event to the patient or family, with the charge nurse or medical director present [1].

**Follow-up:**
- Every Level 1 and Level 2 event gets a root cause analysis. QPS charters the RCA team within 72 hours, and the RCA must be completed within 45 calendar days of the event becoming known [1].
- Completed RCAs go to the Patient Safety Committee, chaired by Dr. Kenji Watanabe, which meets monthly [1].

**Separate case:** If the event is a privacy incident, such as a misdirected fax or a lost device, it goes to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours, by email to privacy@halcyon.example or through the compliance hotline [2].

I didn't search Northwind's `/incident declare` process, so I can't say how it works there.

Northwind uses blameless postmortems for its serious incidents, which is close to a just-culture approach. The stated focus is on the system and process rather than individuals, and names appear only in the incident timeline [1].

**Who writes it:** The incident commander picks the author, usually the responder who knew the most about the failure [1]. Postmortems are due within five business days of resolution for every SEV-1 and SEV-2 [1][2], and they are reviewed at the Thursday reliability meeting [1].

For example, the INC-2291 postmortem (a SEV-1 ingest outage) lists Priya Raman as author, "with the ingest team" [3]. The incident commander for that incident was Oluwaseun Adeyemi [2].

I didn't find a separate just-culture policy for Northwind, so "blameless" is the term the documents use. Their description of the review process matches your RCA approach in its focus on systems, but I can't confirm that the two frameworks are identical.

Northwind has a periodic review with an automatic default, but the knowledge base doesn't show a comparable sign-off process for Halcyon's EHR access.

**Northwind Labs:** Yes. Its information security policy says quarterly access reviews are run by each team lead, and access that is not re-confirmed is revoked automatically [3]. So if nobody signs off, the access is removed rather than left in place. The policy also sets other limits: production access goes through Teleport and expires after 8 hours, with no standing production database access, and access to customer data needs a ticket linked to a support case or incident [3].

**Halcyon Health:** The knowledge base describes monthly compliance reviews of EHR access logs, using automated anomaly detection. Unusual access triggers a review with the employee's manager [1]. It also says clinical system access is suspended automatically if HIPAA training is more than 14 days overdue [1]. I did not find a documented recurring check that asks whether each user still needs their EHR access, or a rule for what happens if no one confirms it. Your compliance team may want to confirm whether that exists outside the knowledge base.

Northwind's knowledge base doesn't say how long the `#vendor-review` process takes. It only says that any tool that will process customer data must clear that review first [1]. The Halcyon requirements below apply to Halcyon staff, not Northwind, so they only matter for your question if the tool would be used at Halcyon.

**Halcyon: what's needed before staff use an AI tool with PHI**

Halcyon's approved-tools page says any tool that will handle protected health information needs [8]:

1. A security risk assessment.
2. A signed business associate agreement (BAA) with the vendor.
3. An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory.
4. For clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO.

Requests go to the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) at privacy@halcyon.example [8]. The typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [8].

Other Halcyon rules that apply:
- PHI may only be stored in approved systems. Putting it in AI tools that aren't on the approved list is prohibited [10].
- "De-identified" doesn't count as a workaround. Treat any patient details as PHI [8].
- Halcyon Assist is approved only for policy questions and must not receive patient details [8].

**Example:** Quillon Ambient, the AI scribe pilot, has an executed BAA dated July 30, 2026 and a completed risk assessment from July 2026 [9]. It is limited to the Riverside and Elm Park clinics, with patient verbal consent at every visit and clinician sign-off on every note [8][9]. Expansion beyond the pilot needs a CSCAB decision and a clinical safety review [9].

The equivalent is the system steward for the owning team. The Halcyon app is owned by Digital Health Engineering — Patient Engagement (DHE-PE), whose steward is Felix Brandt [6][1].

Steward approval is enough on its own for a purely cosmetic change. Halcyon's policy classes cosmetic changes as minor, and minor changes need steward approval only [1]. Significant changes need three things: the steward's approval, clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO (Dr. Anjali Rao, or her delegate Dr. Benedict Osei), and review at the weekly CSCAB [1]. Those rules apply to patient-facing automation, the patient app's clinical content, medication information, orders, results routing, and similar items [1]. A bill-pay layout tweak doesn't appear to fall into those categories, so it should count as minor.

Two caveats:
- If the tweak touches anything beyond appearance, such as the automation behind the screen or any clinical content, it would become a significant change and need the full process [1].
- I'm inferring the classification from the policy's wording. Confirm with Felix Brandt that the change is minor before you ship it.

**Northwind Labs (October invoices, INC-2340):** The fix makes invoice creation idempotent. Invoice creation now uses an idempotency key per workspace and billing period, so a re-run can't create a second invoice for the same period [6][9]. The engineer's Slack notes say the root cause was a payment-provider webhook that timed out, which made the retry logic re-run the batch [7]. The fix shipped October 8, and a dry run afterward produced zero duplicates [7][9].

Northwind also added two follow-ups:
- A daily reconciliation report comparing invoices against charges, marked done [9].
- An alert for when the provider webhook times out during a billing batch. This one is still open, due November 6 [9].

**Halcyon Health (September reminders, IR-0412):** The fix is also an idempotency key, this time on each reminder, keyed on patient, medication and scheduled time. A reminder whose key already exists is never sent again [1]. The root cause was a September 2 scheduler cutover in which the old and new job runners were both active, and neither checked whether a reminder had already gone out [1].

Halcyon also made process changes. Scheduler cutovers now require a written runbook that states how double-running is prevented, and that rule was adopted from this incident [1][2]. Patient-facing automation changes need steward approval, clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO, and review at CSCAB [2]. The reminder text was also changed to say "If you already took this dose, you don't need to take it again" [1].

**Northwind Labs:** Coverage starts on your first day. The welcome guide lists "Health, dental and vision coverage starts on your first day" [2].

**Halcyon Health:** Coverage starts on the first of the month after your start date. This applies to medical, dental and vision [1].

**Northwind Labs has a change freeze over the holidays. Halcyon Health does not have an IT change freeze.**

**Northwind Labs**
- **Holiday freeze: December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027.** Only standard and emergency changes ship [3]. Normal changes, such as schema migrations, infrastructure config, retention changes, and auth or billing logic changes, are blocked [3].
- **Rollbacks are allowed at any time, freeze or not** [3][8].
- **Month-end billing freeze:** no normal changes to Ledger from the last business day of the month until invoices go out, usually the 2nd [3]. The current window started Friday, October 30, and runs until invoices are expected on November 2 [5].
- The deploy window is Monday through Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific, and Friday deploys need on-call engineering manager approval [8].

**Halcyon Health**
- The Juniper steering committee notes say there is "no IT freeze at Halcyon." Clinic managers did ask that pilot training not land in the week of December 21 [4].
- Changes still need normal approvals. Significant changes need the system steward, CMIO clinical safety sign-off, and CSCAB review, and CSCAB meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [1].
- Dates to plan around: a CSCAB slot for the Juniper pilot on December 9 [6], and the Juniper pilot go/no-go on December 16 [4].

If you're changing Ledger or Keystone, also note that Harriet and Arjun are both out November 24–27 [5]. Normal Northwind changes in that window need a plan or the exceptions route, which is the VP Engineering if the approver and delegate are both unavailable [3][5].

**Err high in both cases.** At Northwind, when you're unsure, declare the incident at the higher severity, since downgrading is cheap [1]. At Halcyon, when you're unsure, report the event at the higher level [2].

**Who can change the rating later:**

- **Northwind:** The incident commander (IC) can raise or lower the severity at any time [1]. The person who declares the incident picks the initial severity [1].
- **Halcyon:** Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) reclassifies events if needed [2]. The policy owner is QPS and it is approved by the Patient Safety Committee [2]. A Halcyon example shows this in practice: an event was classified as a Level 2 adverse event, and QPS led the root cause analysis [6].

**Northwind's helpdesk vendor (Hollowpine Software Co.)** is held up by a disagreement over model training. The main open point is Hollowpine's right to use ticket content to train its reply-suggestion model. The DPA draft arrived in July 2026, and redlines have been with legal since August [2]. Hollowpine is running under security exception SEC-EX-117, approved August 24, 2026, and AI reply suggestions must stay disabled until the DPA is signed [2]. The contract renews January 31, 2027 [2].

**Halcyon's patient survey vendor (Tallgrass Survey Co.)** is held up by a data retention dispute in its business associate agreement (BAA). Tallgrass wants to keep identifiable survey responses for 5 years for benchmarking, while Halcyon will accept 18 months [1]. The Privacy Officer, Margaret Holloway, is due to send revised retention language by November 6, 2026 [1]. The security risk assessment passed with conditions in September 2026, and the signed order form is on hold until the BAA is executed [1]. If the BAA isn't signed by January 31, 2027, Quality & Patient Safety will look at other survey vendors [1]. No PHI can be shared with Tallgrass before signing, including for pilots [1]. Until then, Juniper uses the in-app survey [1][6].

Halcyon's offer is bigger: a 20% prompt-pay discount for self-pay patients who pay in full on the day [3], versus Northwind's 15% discount for annual prepayment on Growth [1][2]. The two aren't directly comparable, though, because they apply to different things.

- **Northwind:** Annual prepayment on the Growth plan ($1,200/month list) earns 15%, equal to $12,240 per year [1]. The October 2026 sales memo confirms the 15% prepayment discount is unchanged [2].
- **Halcyon:** Self-pay patients who pay at the time of service and pay in full that day get 20% off [3]. Standard self-pay rates are $165 for a new patient visit, $120 for an established visit, $79 for telehealth and $195 for an annual physical [3].
- **Halcyon exception:** The 20% does not apply to vaccines and injectables, which are already priced at cost plus administration [4]. Sliding-fee patients get the program discount instead [3][4].

**Northwind Labs:** The incident commander (IC) can approve an emergency change during a declared incident, including changes that would normally need the owning team's change approver [1][3]. The IC is paged when someone runs `/incident declare`, and for a SEV-1 an IC must be assigned within 15 minutes [3]. The change is then reviewed retroactively by the owning team's change approver within two business days [1]. If the emergency change is a deploy that would skip the normal bake, the IC can use `/deploy expedite`, which is logged in `#eng-changes` [7]. Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 also gets a blameless postmortem within five business days of resolution [3].

**Halcyon Health:** The on-call medical director may approve an emergency change, but only to stop ongoing patient harm [2]. The on-call medical director is reached through the Halcyon answering service at 555-0144, option 2 [4]. The Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) reviews the change at its next meeting [2]. CSCAB meets weekly on Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [2]. The sources don't specify a deadline for that review.
